subject: Climate & Environment
title: Microplastics Everywhere
description: Learn Microplastics Everywhere in one minute.

hook.text: Microplastics have been found in Arctic ice, deep ocean trenches, and human blood.

buildup.text: Plastic doesn't biodegrade. Instead it breaks into smaller and smaller fragments over time.

discovery.text: Pieces smaller than 5 millimeters are called microplastics. They're in water, air, and soil.

twist.text: A recent study found the average person ingests about a credit card's worth of plastic per week.

climax.text: Scientists are only beginning to understand what microplastics do inside the human body.

punchline.text: We made plastic part of everything — including ourselves.

quiz.question: How small must a plastic fragment be to count as a microplastic?

details.summary: Microplastics are plastic fragments smaller than five millimeters found in oceans, rivers, soil, food, and even human blood. They originate from degrading larger plastics, synthetic clothing fibers, tire wear, and industrial processes.
details.whyItMatters: Microplastics have infiltrated every environment on Earth, including human bodies. The full health implications are still unknown, making this a major emerging environmental and health concern.
takeaways: Microplastics are found in water, soil, air, and human tissue
Synthetic clothing and tire wear are major sources
Health effects of chronic exposure are still being studied

faq.question: How do microplastics enter the human body?
faq.answer: Through drinking water, food especially seafood, and inhaled air. Studies have detected microplastics in human blood, lungs, liver, and placentas. Bottled water contains more microplastics than tap water due to leaching from plastic containers.

faq.question: Can microplastics be filtered out of water?
faq.answer: Conventional water treatment removes some microplastics but not all. Advanced filtration like activated carbon and ultrafiltration membranes are more effective. Washing machine filters can capture synthetic fibers at the source before they enter wastewater.
